clue.text: First light haystack, then run into farm animal

indicators.note: one thing run into another ends up inside it, so these letters go within the animal

blocks.note: a haycock is a small conical heap of hay
a cow is a farm animal
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A farm day starts at dawn among the haystacks, then someone runs into a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: A haycock is an old word for a small haystack. The run goes inside the cow, and the haystack comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockcrow is the time the cockerel crows at dawn, so it is a poetic name for daybreak.

clue.text: Stuff to prepare hastily for the paper

blocks.note: first meaning: pack something tightly in
second meaning: study intensively just before an exam

explanation.surface: Someone hurriedly stuffs things together for the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The paper' suggests a newspaper; it is an exam paper, the thing students revise for at the last minute.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both forcing things into a space and last-minute studying, which packs facts into the head.

clue.text: Leaves for snow caps of Caucasus or Central Asia

indicators.note: a cap sits on top, so each word gives just its opening letter

blocks.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Mountain foliage gives way to snow on the peaks of the Caucasus or Central Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: Snow is slang for cocaine, and the caps are not snowcaps but capital letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Coca is the South American shrub whose leaves are the raw material for cocaine, nicknamed snow.

clue.text: Bothered to grip one of the clubs perhaps taken with driver

indicators.note: gripping something means holding it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: if you bothered about something, you cared
the jack is one card of the clubs suit, among others

explanation.surface: A golfer bothered to grip one of the clubs, perhaps the driver.
explanation.walkthrough: The clubs and driver point to golf; the clubs are a suit of cards, and the driver is the person at the wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A carjacked vehicle is seized by force, often while its driver is still inside it.

clue.text: Bring a friend from time to time

blocks.note: to occasion something is to bring it about
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: Every now and then, bring a friend along.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an invitation; 'bring' is the formal verb meaning to cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Occasionally means now and then, at irregular intervals: an exact adverbial synonym.

clue.text: Female with light coat’s observed in cinema

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
a lick of paint is a thin, light coat of it
the possessive ending supplies the letter as written

explanation.surface: A woman in a pale coat is spotted at the pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light coat' looks like clothing, but here it is a quick coat of paint, a lick.
explanation.definitionFit: The flicks is informal British slang for the movies, from the flickering of early film projection.

clue.text: Drop in returns putting one in the shade

indicators.note: putting one thing in another places it inside, here inside the visit
something that returns goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to drop in on someone is to call on them
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A drop in tax returns leaves one overshadowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting one in the shade' reads as the idiom for outshining someone; 'shade' alone is the definition, a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilac is a pale purple colour named after the flowering shrub, so it is a shade.

clue.text: Huge blow when deducted points go to the other side in sport

indicators.note: points that are deducted are taken away, so those letters come off the storm

blocks.note: a cyclone is a violent storm wind
N and E are compass points
to cross is to go over to the other side

explanation.surface: A massive punch lands when penalty points switch sides in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: The scoring talk suggests penalty points in a game; they are compass points, struck from the end of a wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyclo-cross is a form of bicycle racing over rough off-road circuits, with riders often carrying their bikes.

clue.text: Explorer’s knife roughly made out by leader of search-party

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front, so only that one is used

blocks.note: first letter
to hack is to cut roughly, as with a knife
to let on is to make out or pretend, as in 'he let on he was ill'

explanation.surface: A search-party leader fashions an explorer's knife by hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knife' is a verb here, and 'made out' means pretended, not crafted.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Ernest Shackleton was the Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer who led the Endurance expedition of 1914 to 1917.

clue.text: Verity’s gold-bound mini-volume, lively and entertaining

indicators.note: something bound is wrapped around, so the gold letters enclose what follows

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
cc, cubic centimetres, is a small unit of volume
racy writing is lively and entertaining

explanation.surface: A small gold-bound book belonging to someone called Verity proves lively reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Verity looks like a woman's name owning the book; it is the definition, with ’s meaning 'is'. The mini-volume is not a booklet but a cubic-centimetre measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Verity means truthfulness or correctness, which is what accuracy names: conformity with the facts.

clue.text: Girl one spies across pond by a lake

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the map abbreviation for lake
the Roman numeral for one
the CIA is the American spy agency, across the Atlantic 'pond' from Britain

explanation.surface: A girl watches someone spying across a pond beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One spies across pond' sounds like a person peering over water; the pond is the Atlantic, so the spies are American. The letters for 'a lake' are placed by, here in front of, the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Alicia is a girl's given name, the Spanish and Latinate form of Alice.

clue.text: Take casing for electric clutch roughly, fetching pipe down

indicators.note: a casing is the outside of something, so only the two outer letters are used
done roughly means not in proper order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fitting a cover on an electric clutch, a mechanic tells a colleague to shut up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' looks like an instruction, but it is the first slice of the letters to be jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Cut the cackle is a British idiom meaning stop chattering, the same order as pipe down or be quiet.

clue.text: Tap round key in unusual musical timepiece

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement is a non-standard one, so all these letters are reordered

blocks.note: a cock is a tap or valve, as in stopcock
E is one of the musical keys A to G
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tap a key on a strange clock that plays music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical timepiece' looks like the definition, but the musical word is raw material. The tap, the key and the word all go into one big rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A caesium clock is the atomic clock that keeps world standard time, by counting oscillations of caesium atoms.

clue.text: Poor creatures that are moved around on prayer mats?

definitions.text: that are moved around on prayer mats?

blocks.note: first meaning: from the saying 'as poor as a church mouse'

blocks.clueFragment: that are moved around on prayer mats?
blocks.note: second meaning: computer mice slide on mats, and a church's mats would be prayer mats

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: a computer mouse moves about on a mouse mat, so a church's would use prayer mats.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially the poorest of creatures, church mice have nothing to eat in a building with no pantry.

clue.text: Doctor going about in a tie’s making for gay bars

indicators.note: going about something means going around it, so these letters wrap the next word

blocks.note: a GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor
taken as written
taken as written
to lace is to tie, as with shoes
the possessive ending supplies the letter as written

explanation.surface: A doctor in a tie is heading for some gay bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gay' is used in its old sense of bright and merry; the bars are pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Gin palaces were the showy, brightly lit Victorian pubs, gaudy bars full of mirrors and gilt.

clue.text: Tug is white, coming from Germany to tour island

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all the way round it, so the wine letters surround the island

blocks.note: hock is British for a white Rhine wine from Germany
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A white tugboat from Germany sets off to sail round an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a tugboat; 'white' is a noun, a German white wine, which the British call hock.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoick is a colloquial British verb for pulling or yanking something up abruptly, a sharp tug.

clue.text: Delegate’s blooming cheek, some might say

indicators.note: what people say is heard, not read, so the spoken form counts here

blocks.note: a flower that is out is in bloom
sauce is cheeky impudence; in a non-rhotic accent it matches the second half

explanation.surface: A delegate is rebuked for their bloody cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' reads as the mild British swear word, but it means flowering. Spoken 'out sauce' gives the answer in British pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: To outsource work is to contract it to outsiders, handing over a task much as one delegates it.

clue.text: Used train to arrive at square

blocks.note: used goods are old, second-hand
to school a horse or pupil is to train it

explanation.surface: Someone took the train to reach a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' looks like a place to arrive at; it is the slang adjective for unfashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone square is conventional and unfashionable, and old-school describes traditional, old-fashioned ways.

clue.text: Spurn introduction to restaurant critic’s piece on dessert?

blocks.note: re means 'on the subject of', as in a letter heading
pud is British slang for pudding
a food critic's review might well open with 'I ate...'

explanation.surface: Snubbing a restaurant critic's piece about puddings before even reading the introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: Imagine the critic's column headed 'Re pud' and starting 'I ate'. 'Introduction to restaurant' tempts you to take only its first letter, but nothing needs it.
explanation.definitionFit: To repudiate is to reject or disown something, refusing to accept it: a formal synonym for scorning it.

clue.text: One might get down to this business of investigating?

definitions.text: One might get down to this

blocks.note: a DI, Detective Inspector, is the British police officer running an investigation
'X of Y' is turned round into the possessive 'Y's X'
Co. is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: Detectives settle down to the serious business of an investigation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get down to business' is the familiar idiom, but 'get down' here is slang for dancing. 'Business of investigating' reads as the detective inspector's company.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is a club or party playing pop music for dancing, and 'get down' is slang for dancing energetically.

clue.text: Fellow netting in a locally organised league once

indicators.note: netting a fish means catching it inside a net, so one piece encloses another
something organised has been put into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: he, a male person, stands for a fellow
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man joins a parish league that was organised in the neighbourhood long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' tempts you toward F or MAN; it is the pronoun he, wrapped round 'in' before everything is rearranged with 'a locally'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy Alliance was the 1815 coalition of Russia, Austria and Prussia, a historical league of monarchies.

clue.text: Annoying to be deprived of goods as tips spent

indicators.note: being deprived of something means losing it, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: galling means annoying, vexing
G is the abbreviation for goods, taken off at each tip of the word

explanation.surface: It is annoying to have your goods taken when the tips have all been spent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' looks like gratuities; it means the two ends of the word, each of which is a G.
explanation.definitionFit: All-in is British informal for exhausted, completely worn out, as a spent runner is.

clue.text: Bows, a bit upset, withdrawing quietly

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned over, so the letters run bottom to top
withdrawing something takes it out, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: a scrap is a small bit
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Someone bows, a little upset, and quietly leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a person bowing; bows here are curves, and quietly is the musical p.
explanation.definitionFit: A bow is a curved shape, like an archer's bow, so bows and arcs are both curves.

clue.text: Lead ball ultimately something used to pot swallows

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so the final letter is taken
what is swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a cue is used to pot balls in snooker or pool
final letter

explanation.surface: A lead ball is something you might pot with a snooker cue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like the metal; it is a pointer or hint. To pot a ball is to send it into a pocket on a snooker table.
explanation.definitionFit: A lead in a police inquiry is a clue: a piece of evidence that points toward the solution.

clue.text: The state of New Jersey’s carrier?

definitions.text: The state of New Jersey’s carrier?

blocks.note: surface reading: the American state on the east coast
setter's reading: the condition of a cow carrying a new Jersey, a calf of that dairy breed

explanation.walkthrough: 'State of New Jersey' is an American state, until you read state as condition and a new Jersey as an unborn calf of the Channel Island cattle breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A pregnant cow is described as being with calf, the farming phrase for its condition while carrying a young one.

clue.text: Shooting scene that’s wheeled out from popular rock opera

indicators.note: the letters are lifted out of the run of words that follows
to wheel round is to turn back the other way, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the next two

explanation.surface: A gunfight scene is wheeled on stage in a hit rock opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular' tempts you to IN or POP; it is just part of the letter string, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The O.K. Corral in Tombstone, Arizona, was the site of the famous 1881 gunfight involving Wyatt Earp.

clue.text: Becoming less like home, last of the grand houses

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
to house something is to hold it inside, so the outer letters wrap the rest

blocks.note: final letter of the word
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
as means like, in comparisons
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: The grandest stately home has grown less homely.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition breaks off after 'less', not after 'home'. The final letter of 'the' and the grand go on either side of 'like home'.
explanation.definitionFit: Easing means lessening or diminishing, as pain or tension does when it relaxes.

clue.text: Girls briefly follow Jan’s predecessor, standing down

indicators.note: a word said briefly is cut short, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: December comes before January; Dec is its abbreviation
lasses are girls, in northern English and Scots

explanation.surface: Some girls follow a man called Jan's predecessor as he steps down from office.
explanation.walkthrough: Jan looks like a person, perhaps the next holder of an office; it is January, so the predecessor is the previous month.
explanation.definitionFit: Déclassé means fallen in social status or rank, so one's standing has gone down.
